summary:
Consensual, private, non-commercial same-sex sexual activity between adults has been lawful in Guatemala since 1871.

Guatemala provides no legal gender recognition. Since 2016 a person may change a legal name to match gender identity only with judicial permission; legal gender cannot be changed, and a person cannot self-report gender for official documents, which must show the sex and name assigned at birth. The resulting mismatch between presentation and identity documents exposes a trans visitor to scrutiny during identity checks, and the same mismatch obstructs residents' access to government services that require official identification.

Guatemala is bound by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion OC-24/17 of 9 January 2018, which holds recognition of gender identity on official documents to be a human right under the American Convention on Human Rights and requires states parties to grant same-sex couples access to all existing domestic family registration systems, including marriage with all rights deriving from marriage. The inventory contains no record of Guatemalan compliance with that opinion.

Guatemalan law recognises no marriage, civil union or domestic partnership for same-sex couples. A civil unions bill introduced in December 2016 by Deputy Sandra Morán has not been debated since.

Legislative efforts to reverse what protections exist have been sustained. A December 2017 bill to recognise the right to gender identity and allow transgender people to change name and gender on birth certificates was rejected in August 2018 by both the Legislative and Constitutional Points Commission and the Women's Commission; a later gender identity bill was advocated without enactment. Initiative No. 5940, received by the Legislative Directorate on 12 July 2021 and presented to the plenary on 13 September 2021, proposed a law guaranteeing the integral protection of children and adolescents against gender identity disorders. Initiative 5490 advanced in December 2021 to remove education about transgender individuals in schools on grounds of protecting children from gender identity disorders and to require censorship of media featuring transgender individuals, winning unanimous approval from the Congress education committee before full congress review. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2022 that such bills would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.

The Life and Protection bill, Initiative 5272, would increase penalties for abortion, explicitly ban same-sex marriage, define the family as a father, a mother and children, and describe homosexuality as contrary to biology and genetics. It passed first and second readings and its third reading was blocked in September 2018 with no debate since. Congress approved the Law for the Protection of Life and Family on 8 March 2022; after President Alejandro Giammattei announced on 11 March that he would veto it as violating the Constitution and international agreements, Congress archived and discarded the law on 15 March 2022 by 119 votes, leaving its prohibitions without effect.

Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations, and the penal code's prohibition of discrimination does not explicitly cover gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. A May 2017 bill to add gender identity to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 as a protected category remains unadopted. No convictions for discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds are recorded through 2021. Bias-motivated crimes on the basis of gender identity are reportedly tolerated by the government, particularly where harassment or violence is directed at transgender people, and the law provides no hate-crime protection.

Central American governments have long excluded trans women from femicide protections, and Guatemalan officials have justified that exclusion by stating that transgender women are not biological women. The exclusion is official.

As of 2020 the prison system placed trans women in men's prisons, facilitating anti-trans violence and exposure to sexual assault. Bárbara Herrarte, a trans activist with Redmmutrans, described her time in a men's prison: always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him. The record shows no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on trans custody. The LGBTQ organisation Lambda flags forced internal displacement from violence.

Conversion practices are normalised, including among mental health professionals, and operate alongside documented electroshock therapy in active Evangelical-funded centres mainly in rural areas. Corrective rape is prosecuted only as rape, not as a hate crime. Late-1990s United Nations and NGO reports documented systematic targeting of LGBT people for death as part of a social cleansing campaign, which included the 1997 gunning down in Guatemala City of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia.

Guatemala is one of four countries where the Inter-American Court's 2017 gender-identity opinion advanced legal gender recognition while a vociferous opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms foments backlash, according to an Arcus Foundation report of May 2024. Despite the election of a more progressive government in 2024, Congress remained predominantly conservative with no significant pro-LGBTIQ initiatives, and in August 2025 it hosted the Meeting for Religious Freedom, Life and Family in Congress to advance an anti-LGBTIQ agenda.
tangentialFactors:
A majority of Guatemalans affiliate with the Catholic Church or Pentecostal churches, and attitudes towards LGBT people tend to reflect prevailing religious mores. Those faiths have traditionally upheld socially conservative positions and in particular tend to treat homosexuality and cross-dressing as signs of immorality, a view reflected in the dominant political parties, while most other parties generally ignore LGBT rights.

Negative social attitudes have persisted despite legality since 1871, with documented harassment and targeted killings of LGBT people. Only one gay bar was permitted from 1976 until the late 1990s, a period that coincides with the growth of the fundamentalist Pentecostal population.

Openly LGBT political representation began with lesbian Deputy Sandra Morán elected in January 2016 and gay Deputy Aldo Dávila elected in June 2019, both on platforms to criminalize hate crimes and hate speech against the LGBT community. Former President Álvaro Colom supported civil unions, while President Jimmy Morales supported the marriage ban proposal.

The Arcus Foundation places the country alongside El Salvador, Honduras and Mexico as one of four states where the 2017 regional gender-identity opinion advanced recognition while binary-definition opposition organised against it.
